item.text: {"text":"Recent evidence supports human-calibrated recommendation diagnostics. [Penha et al. (2025–2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.23312) find that richer metadata and longer histories improve automated relevance judgments, but item-level agreement remains moderate despite strong aggregate system-ranking agreement. [LARA (2025)](https://www.nist.gov/publications/llm-assisted-relevance-assessments) likewise favors combining human and automated assessments because judge performance can shift across tasks. Neither establishes the requested four-label taxonomy; it should be treated as a proposed rubric requiring local validation.\n\nFor this task, use separate annotation dimensions: relevance—recent-history-specific, broadly related, unrelated, or insufficient evidence—and possible functional redundancy—supported, unsupported, or insufficient evidence. Require each judgment to cite a permitted title/description span and relevant history item; recent-history alignment is evidence of relevance, not proof of current intent. Description overlap can flag possible redundancy but cannot establish ownership, compatibility, or lack of need. Calibrate proxies against explicit feedback from the twenty users, preserving disagreements rather than replacing user judgments. Report category-level confusion matrices, raw agreement, nominal Cohen’s κ, sample sizes, and abstention rates; distinguish missing user feedback from automated abstention. Freeze the rubric before assessment and separate calibration examples from evaluation examples where feasible. [Rao and Callison-Burch (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00093) show that exclusions, abstentions, pooling, and judgment scales can substantially change reported agreement without changing verdicts. Publish denominators and coverage alongside conditional agreement, with uncertainty clustered by user. These diagnostics supplement the fixed macro validation HR@10; they do not replace it."}
